opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think embodied intelligence right now is in a phase that feels a lot like large language models around 2018 or 2019. Everyone can sense that something big is coming, the direction is broadly agreed on, but nobody has yet found the equivalent of the "scaling moment," where you add more data and compute and capability reliably goes up.

If I break it down, the hardware side has actually moved faster than many people expected. Humanoid bodies, dexterous hands, actuators, the cost curve, especially with China's supply chain, have come down dramatically in just a couple of years. A few years ago a decent humanoid was a research artifact. Now you can buy one at a price that makes it realistic for labs and even small companies to run fleets.

The real bottleneck is the brain, and underneath that, data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. Robots don't have an internet of physical interaction. So the field is trying several paths at once: teleoperation data collection, simulation and sim-to-real, learning from human videos, and these vision-language-action models that borrow priors from big multimodal models. Each one has a piece of the answer, but none of them alone has shown clean scaling laws for general manipulation yet.

So my honest assessment is: demos are ahead of reality. You see very impressive videos, robots folding clothes, doing backflips, but the gap between a curated demo and something that works reliably for eight hours a day in an unstructured home or factory is still large. Generalization, robustness, and long-horizon tasks are where things break.

That said, I'm optimistic. I think the next two to three years will decide whether we find a data flywheel, where deployed robots doing useful, if narrow, work generate the data that makes them more general. Whoever closes that loop first will have something like a GPT moment for the physical world. We're not there yet, but we're closer than at any point before.

r001.rationale: It compares embodied intelligence’s current phase to large language models in 2018 or 2019, conveying a stage comparable to GPT-1.

r002.rationale: It says the field has not found a “scaling moment” where adding data and compute reliably increases capability.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say we're at the stage where the demos have gotten ahead of the deployments, and that gap is the whole story right now.

If you look at the surface, it's an incredibly exciting moment. The humanoids walk convincingly, the dexterous hands fold laundry on camera, and every few weeks there's a new foundation model trained on robot data that generalizes a bit further than the last one. Capital is pouring in, and the narrative is that embodied AI is where large language models were around 2020, right before the inflection.

But I think that analogy is misleading in one crucial way. Language models had the internet as a free, enormous, already-collected dataset. Robots don't have that. Every piece of real interaction data has to be generated by a physical system touching the physical world, and that's slow, expensive, and messy. So the field is really in a data-bootstrapping phase. We're trying teleoperation, we're trying simulation, we're trying to learn from human video, and nobody has fully solved how to get from millions of trajectories to the billions you probably need.

The second honest thing to say is that reliability, not capability, is the bottleneck. A robot that does a task correctly ninety percent of the time looks amazing in a video and is nearly useless in a factory or a home. Getting that last few percent is where most of the engineering lifetime goes, and it doesn't photograph well, so it's underappreciated.

So my assessment is this: we're past the point where it's a research curiosity, and we're clearly before the point where it's an industry with repeatable economics. The next two or three years will be decided less by who has the best model and more by who finds a narrow, real scenario, gets to high reliability there, and uses that to generate the data flywheel. The companies that treat this as a product problem rather than a demo problem are the ones I'd bet on.

r001.rationale: The response compares embodied AI to language models around 2020, but does not characterize its stage as comparable to GPT-1.

r002.rationale: It says the field is in a data-bootstrapping phase and that nobody has fully solved how to scale from millions of trajectories to the billions likely needed.

astra-6.text:
I think embodied intelligence is still at an early stage, but we’re moving from demonstrations toward testing whether these systems can do useful work reliably. We can already see robots performing impressive tasks. The harder question is whether they can repeat those tasks when the environment changes, recover when something goes wrong, and operate at an acceptable cost.

I’d distinguish between a compelling demo and a practical product. A demo can succeed under carefully prepared conditions. A product has to handle variations in lighting, objects, people, and the task itself. That gap is still substantial.

My view is that progress will first become tangible in more constrained settings, where the tasks are clear and success can be measured. Those deployments can also generate experience that helps improve the systems. General-purpose robots operating freely in homes are a much higher bar.

So I’m optimistic, but I’d judge this stage less by how humanlike a robot looks and more by how consistently it can complete useful tasks without intervention.

r001.rationale: The response calls embodied intelligence early-stage but does not compare it to GPT-1.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability, constrained deployments, and the product gap, but does not state that no recipe for scalable development has been found.

sol-6.1.text:
I think embodied intelligence is still at an early stage, but we’re moving from demonstrations toward testing whether these systems can actually do useful work. A robot completing a task once is exciting; completing it reliably, in a changing environment, at an acceptable cost is a much higher bar.

The key question is how well the whole system works together: perception, decision-making, and physical control. In the physical world, an error changes the situation you have to deal with next. The robot needs to recognize that and recover, rather than simply follow a sequence of actions.

So I’m optimistic, but I would judge progress by reliability and adaptability. Can it handle an unfamiliar object? Can it recover when a grasp fails? How often does a person need to intervene? I expect useful applications in constrained settings to come before broadly capable robots that can work anywhere.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls embodied intelligence “still at an early stage” but does not compare its development to GPT-1.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses reliability, adaptability, and constrained applications, but does not state that no recipe for scalable development has been found.
